name: Diffusion
kick: generative models · first principles · how to create new realistic data from scratch
title: Diffusion — learning to reverse noise to create new data
lede: To generate a brand-new, realistic image or shape, you need to produce something the model has never seen before. The space of all possible images is astronomically large — how do you learn which ones are good? Diffusion is a radical reframing: instead of learning to build good samples from scratch, destroy a real image with noise step by step until it is pure random static, then learn to undo that process. Train a network to take one small step backward through noise, then run it in reverse from pure noise to create. Here is the idea, a measurement on a real toy showing it works, why undoing small steps is cleverer than building whole samples at once, where it stumbles, and how this idea powers the image generators behind every modern AI art tool.

sections.h2: 1 · The problem — generating new realistic data is astronomically hard

blocks.html: When you want to create a new image or shape or piece of text, you are choosing from a space so enormous that most random guesses are garbage. If you tried to build an image pixel by pixel, the odds of landing on something realistic are essentially zero — the space is too big, the rules too intricate. A model that learned to make good samples needs to have found the tiny sliver of space where realistic things live, then learned to sample from only there. That is an extraordinarily hard problem stated forward.
So the need is sharp: is there a way to reframe generation as a simpler problem — one a neural network can actually learn?

sections.h2: 2 · The reframe — destroy structure, then learn to restore it

blocks.html: The radical move. Take a real image or shape. Add noise to it — a little random static sprinkled across it. Then add more noise. Keep going until after 50 steps or 1,000 steps, all the structure is gone: it is pure random garbage, indistinguishable from static. That forward process — adding noise step by step — is trivial. Anybody can do it. It requires no learning.

Now flip it. Train a neural network to do the reverse: given a noisy image partway through that noise-adding process, predict what noise was just added, and subtract it. If the network learns this one-step backwards move well, you can run it in reverse from the end: start with pure noise, have the network remove one step of noise, then remove one more step, and so on. After 50 iterations, pure random static has been shaped into a realistic sample. The hard problem of 'make a good image from scratch' becomes a chain of tiny, tractable steps: 'guess and remove the noise I just added.'

That is diffusion. The key is that each small step is easy to learn — predicting noise added in one step is within reach of a neural network. Chaining many of them together accomplishes something that looked impossible: creating brand-new, realistic data from pure randomness.

sections.h2: 3 · Seen on a real run — noise goes from zero success to 97 percent on target

blocks.html: We built a simple toy: a 2-dimensional space with 8 Gaussian blobs arranged on a ring. The question: can pure noise land on one of those blobs by chance? Can a network learn to denoise noise back onto them? We trained a network to reverse a 50-step noising process and compared.

blocks.caption: Samples landing on the target shape (8 Gaussians on a ring). Pure noise, then after learning to reverse 50 steps of noise.

blocks.html: The discovered fact: pure noise lands on the target shape zero percent of the time. After training a network to reverse the 50-step noise process, generated samples land on it 97 percent of the time. The same network, given noise and asked to denoise, reliably steers random static into a shape the model has learned.

sections.h2: 4 · Why learning to undo noise teaches a model to generate

blocks.html: The insight is that denoising is a direct window into the data distribution. When you learn to undo one step of noise at every point in space, you are learning: where does the data sit? Which direction is toward realistic data? By removing noise repeatedly, the network makes thousands of tiny nudges, and those nudges accumulate. Each one is a small step toward the high-density regions where real data lives.

This works because noise is a smooth process. A single step of noise is not too different from the previous state — the network can see both in its input (the noisy image and the noise added) and learn the pattern. But collectively, 50 or 1,000 steps of denoising act like a learnable map from the outside (pure randomness) to the inside (realistic data). No hand-written rule describes what 'good data' looks like; the network infers it from the denoising task alone.

sections.h2: 5 · The one real weakness — generation needs many sequential steps

blocks.html: The catch is speed. To generate a single image, you must run the network 50, 100, or even 1,000 times, once per denoising step. Each run costs compute. For real applications this is slow — it can take tens of seconds or minutes to generate a single image, where a discriminative model (one that only recognizes) runs in milliseconds. That sequential cost is why a whole research industry has emerged around faster alternatives: flow matching (learning a smooth path from noise to data in fewer steps) and distillation (training a smaller network to mimic a trained diffusion model in just 4 steps) both attack this bottleneck.

sections.h2: 6 · The surprise — this powers image generators used by millions

blocks.html: This simple idea — destroy structure, learn to restore it — when scaled to millions of images and billions of learned numbers, becomes the engine of Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, and every modern AI image generator. The same logic applies to audio and video: you can corrupt a sound with noise, learn to denoise it, and sample new audio by running the reverse process. The trick of breaking a hard problem into many easy steps, stacked in sequence, is now central to generative AI. Cousin ideas like score matching (learn the direction toward data) and flow matching (learn a smooth path) refine the strategy. And guidance adds a steering mechanism: nudge the denoising toward a specific class or description. This single reframing — that generation is denoising — made AI art possible.

sections.h2: 7 · Where it is used in practice — creating realistic images, videos, and audio by learning to reverse noise

blocks.html: Image generators like Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, and similar tools create new images by starting with pure noise and gradually removing it. Video generation systems use the same approach to create new video frames. Audio synthesis systems (music generation, voice synthesis) create sound by reversing a process that corrupts clean audio with noise. All of these systems share the same core: they learn to undo destruction, then run the reverse process to create.

During training, the model takes real data (an image, audio, video) and adds noise step by step until it is pure random. Then it trains a network to predict and subtract the noise that was just added, reversing one step at a time. At generation time, the model starts with pure noise and runs the learned denoising many times in a row. Each step removes a little noise and adds a little structure, and by the end the accumulated steps have shaped random into something realistic.

Breaking the impossible problem of generating good data from scratch into many tiny tractable steps (reverse one layer of noise) is why diffusion models can generate diverse, realistic outputs that other approaches could not.

recipe.summary: Run a toy diffusion model on 8 Gaussians arranged on a 2D ring. First, measure what fraction of pure noise samples land within a small radius of any blob (0%). Train a network to predict and subtract noise at each of 50 steps, reversing a forward noise process. Then, sample by starting from pure noise and running the learned denoising network 50 times. Measure what fraction of generated samples land on the target shape (97%).
recipe.eq:
forward:   x_t = sqrt(alpha_t) * x_0  +  sqrt(1 - alpha_t) * epsilon
reverse:  x_{t-1} = (1/sqrt(alpha_t)) * (x_t - sqrt(1 - alpha_t) * pred_noise)
generate: start with x_T ~ N(0, I),  iterate reverse for t = T, T-1, ..., 1
measured purity:   noise-only 0%,   learned denoising 97%
recipe.note: Full script: scripts/experiments/stanford_diffusion.py (exp_diffusion), the toy 8-Gaussian target. Numbers are the run's output verbatim.
